newsitem.title: UK: Europe issue further threatens British government.
newsitem.headline: Europe issue further threatens British government.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major faces a grim week, with rebel members of his Conservative Party set to take advantage of his lost majority in parliament to press home their attacks about Britain's position in Europe.

He will also have to deal with the troublesome problem of Northern Ireland and is scheduled to meet Irish Prime Minister John Bruton on Monday to discuss a feared Christmas offensive by Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas.

Major went on national television on Sunday to say he would not be bullied over the issue of Europe, but several Conservative "backbenchers" -- members of parliament with no government posts -- vowed to make trouble for him.

Polls show the Conservatives as much as 37 points behind the opposition Labour Party and, in a new blow, the one-time Conservative stronghold of Basildon in Essex indicated it, too, had deserted Major.

The MORI poll for the Sun newspaper showed only 24 percent of voters there would choose Major's party in an election. Support for Labour skyrocketed from 42 percent at the last election in 1992 to 61 percent.
In the 1992 election the voters of Basildon predicted Major's unexpected win with early returns for the Conservatives.

The MORI poll showed that voters nationwide largely supported the rebellious Conservative MPs, with 64 percent opposing British participation in a single European currency. Only 44 percent favoured Britain staying in the European Union.

These are the issues that have split the Conservative Party. Major said he would not be shifted from a "wait-and-see" policy on Europe, arguing that Britain must keep its hand in negotiations with Brussels.
"We are not going to be held to ransom," Major said.
But the rebellious backbenchers have scented blood.
Major's one-seat parliamentary majority vanished on Friday when Sir John Gorst said he would no longer automatically vote with the government in a row over a hospital closure.
This means his government could be toppled at any time in a parliamentary vote.

Another malcontent, Terry Dicks, told Sky television: "He is going to have to wait and see how I play my hand now...If they had to vote tonight I would have brought the government down and to hell with them."
The government is expected to lose even more with a by-election on Thursday in Barnsley in northern England. Labour is widely expected to take that seat.
The European issue will not cool down anytime soon, either.

A two-day parliamentary debate on Europe starting on Wednesday will give "Eurosceptics" a fresh chance to air their grievances. Then a two-day EU summit starts on Friday in Dublin where other leaders will push for more European integration.
An obviously gleeful Labour Party did not threaten an immediate challenge to Major's government, which can hang on -- just -- with the help of nine Northern Irish Ulster Unionists.
But therein lies another problem for Major. The Ulster Unionists have been pressuring Major to keep the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein out of talks on the future of Northern Ireland.

Irish officials say this means Major can make no concessions on the issue when he meets Bruton on Monday. And that, security sources say, could lead to a new round of IRA attacks in Britain, Northern Ireland and elsewhere.
